insertText.text: 1:10–1:45. WILLINGNESS-TO-PAY RESULT. Each dot is one real visitor; coral dots clicked checkout. 213 visitors, 9 checkout clicks: 4.2%, well under our 10% bar. By price, checkout rates were 2.7% at $129, 4.7% at $169 and 5.3% at $199. 4 of the 9 left an email for the waitlist. What we changed because of this: we removed the price question nobody answered, rebuilt the out-of-stock screen around the waitlist, and added a Show more section and session replays so we can see where people drop off. Data: Nov 12–19 (as of Nov 19, 10:48 PM). Since the last update: 13 more visitors and 6 more checkout clicks.

1:45–2:10. Confidence is low to medium. We are confident most cold visitors will not buy at any of these prices. We are not confident about which price is best: 9 clicks cannot rank three prices, and a click is not a payment. Next we would test a $10 refundable deposit, which is real money; a parent as the payer; a payment plan; and a cheaper version without cellular. Verdict: the model is plausible but not proven. $169 keeps a healthy margin, but demand at that price is unproven.

3:00–3:35. CUSTOMER ACQUISITION RESULT. Paid ads brought 148 of our 213 visitors, about 69% of the traffic, and not one added to cart. Organic Instagram, people who came through the link in our bio, brought 43 visitors and 9 checkout clicks: 20.9%. Other sources brought 22 visitors and 0 checkout clicks. So a cold audience scrolling past an ad does not buy a $169 bracelet on first sight, but people who already follow us do click. What we changed: we moved the shop to a clean link, wearfirefly, because the old one showed a personal GitHub name; we set up a live dashboard that splits every visit by ad and channel; and we are moving effort from cold ads to warm channels. Data: Nov 12–19 (as of Nov 19, 10:48 PM). Since the last update: 13 more visitors and 6 more checkout clicks. FILL IN the ad spend from Instagram before presenting.

3:35–4:00. We are fairly confident that cold paid ads do not convert yet: 148 visitors and zero carts. But it was two ads over a few days, so we have not tested many messages. We are less confident in the organic number: 43 visitors is small, and some are probably friends of the team. Next we would test the warm channels we already tagged: group chats and flyers, a referral code for friend groups, a parent gift ad before the holidays, and showing ads again to people who already visited. Verdict: not a strong go-to-market yet. The channel that converts is small, and the channel that scales does not convert.

4:00–4:35. The product side works. At $169, after about $80 to make, $5 in card fees, $10 shipping and $8 for returns, we keep about $66 per bracelet. It is a one-time purchase, so that $66 is the lifetime value. For a healthy three-to-one ratio we can spend at most $22 to win a customer. If one in three checkout clicks becomes a purchase, that means about $7 per checkout click. Our followers gave us 9 checkout clicks for free, but paid ads produced 0 checkout clicks from 148 visits, so paid acquisition cost is not measurable yet. Conclusion: we would make money on each bracelet, but we have not shown we can buy customers for less than we earn. The math is in the appendix.
